Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

vignette:
Priya was thirty-two years old and had worked as an emergency room nurse for nearly a decade. She had seen a great deal—car accidents, overdoses, cardiac arrests—and had always prided herself on staying calm when everything around her turned chaotic. But nothing had prepared her for the night the mass casualty alert came in. A bomb had been detonated at a community festival three blocks from the hospital. The first wave of victims arrived before the sirens had even stopped. Priya remembered the stretchers pouring through the double doors, but only in flashes: a woman with a tourniquet on what was left of her arm, a man whose face was so covered in soot and blood that his age was impossible to guess, a child who was not making any sound at all. She remembered her own hands moving, setting up IV lines, handing off supplies, but it felt like watching someone else perform those actions. What she could not recall, no matter how hard she tried, was the sequence of events—the minutes and hours blurred into a series of disconnected images that refused to line up. She would begin to replay that night and find herself pushing the memory away before she reached the part she most dreaded, as if her mind slammed a door shut right before the worst moment arrived. And when she did manage to hold onto a fragment, it struck her as so extreme, so far outside the realm of ordinary life, that she could not truly believe it had happened to her. It felt more like a scene from a movie she had once seen, not something she had actually lived.

In the weeks that followed, Priya found herself avoiding the break room where the television was always on, because the news coverage replayed footage of the festival grounds and the sound of helicopters made her chest tighten. At first she told herself she just needed a few days off. Then she started requesting assignments in the quieter parts of the hospital—the outpatient clinic, the administrative wing—anywhere she could be sure she would not hear the overhead page for a trauma team or catch the scent of antiseptic mixed with something metallic. She stopped eating lunch in the cafeteria because the clatter of trays and the sudden bursts of laughter from other nurses felt jarring and wrong, as if they were laughing in a world that no longer existed. Her supervisor noticed and asked if everything was all right. Priya said she was just tired. She did not mention that her sleep had fractured into shallow, watchful intervals, or that she had taken to scanning every crowded room for exits before she could sit down. She had come to believe that if she let her guard down for a moment, something terrible would happen again—not the same disaster, but something equally violent and unexpected, and this time she would not be able to hold herself together. The thought frightened her more than the memory itself.

Her relationships began to thin. Friends invited her to dinners and birthday gatherings, but she declined, certain that she would not be able to fake a normal conversation, that someone would ask about work and she would either say something strange or freeze. One evening her mother called and Priya found herself telling her everything was fine, that she was just busy with overtime, because the alternative—describing the fragments that visited her at odd moments, the way the smell of grilled meat from a neighbor’s barbecue made her nauseous—seemed impossible. She was single and lived alone, which had always suited her, but now the quiet of her apartment felt both a relief and a trap. Some nights she sat on the couch and tried to think through that night in a complete, coherent line, start to finish, but every time she got to the image of the child who had not been crying, her mind went blank and the rest of the story was gone.

What finally brought Priya to the clinic was a morning shift when a code blue was called overhead and she walked into a resuscitation room and saw a patient with a blood pressure cuff still inflated and a tangle of tubing that looked, for a split second, like a field dressing. Her hands began to shake and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she stood gripping the sink and telling herself she was a nurse, she had done this a thousand times, but her reflection looked like a stranger. After that, she made an appointment. She sat in the waiting room with her hands folded, hoping the therapist would understand that her memory felt stolen from someone else’s life, and terrified that if she started talking, the door she had been pushing shut would fly open and she would not be able to close it again.
